deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a German prose page of lecture or study notes on ancient Greek history, continuing from folio 123, which covers Philip II's northern campaigns, the sieges of Perinthus and Byzantium, Elatea and the run-up to Chaeronea. The handwriting is a rounded, fairly juvenile Kurrent hand and does not look like Gauss's. It is probably a family member's or pupil's history notebook bound into the Nachlass.

Content, in order:
(1) At Chaeronea (338 BC) the armies met. Alexander ('Alexander M.' = Magnus) defeated one wing and Philip the other, and Philip thereby subjugated Greece.
(2) Philip then planned to attack Persia. He had already had himself declared supreme commander (hegemon) of the Hellenes, i.e. the League of Corinth, 337 BC.
(3) Just then he fell victim to an assassination.
(4) Background: his consort Olympias, from whom he separated because she was too domineering. He then married Cleopatra, called here 'daughter of his general Attalus'. At that time he married a daughter to Epirus.
(5) At Aegae the festivities were to be held, and at the wedding in 336 a Macedonian, Pausanias, stabbed him in the chest. A cross-reference '+' points to the marginal note '+ im Theater': he was killed in the theatre.
(6) Alexander the Great succeeded him, 'one of the most cultivated and most amiable of men'. 'He had Aristotle as [teacher]' continues on the next page.

There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct.
errors: Historical slip: Cleopatra (Eurydice), Philip's last wife, was the niece (or ward) of Attalus, not his daughter.
The dates 338 and 336 are BC; this is not marked, a minor point for school notes.

Simplification: the narrative of the break with Olympias is moralized. Historically it is tied to Philip's remarriage and to Attalus' insult to Alexander, not simply to her being 'herrschsüchtig' (domineering).
The victim of the dagger thrust is not written explicitly here ('stieß ihm … den Dolch in die Brust'). It is clear from context, but the transcription reads it correctly as 'ihm'.

results.what: Narrative notes on Philip II of Macedon (Chaeronea 338 BC, hegemony, assassination at Aegae 336 BC) and Alexander's succession
results.usually_credited_to: Standard classical sources (Diodorus, Plutarch, Arrian); textbook material

deep.surprise_reason: The page is non-mathematical school-style history notes, apparently not in Gauss's own hand. It contains no mathematical content at all, and the historical content is routine textbook material with one standard confusion (Attalus' niece called his daughter).

checkable.asserts: Two years elapsed between Chaeronea (338 BC) and Philip's assassination (336 BC), consistent with the page's dates (trivial; there is no mathematical content to check).

transcription_corrections: Line 1: the uncertain 'trafen[?] sich hier[?]' may read 'trafen sich beide' (the two armies met). 'trafen' is fairly secure; the second word is uncertain.
Margin note '+ im Theater[?]' is consistent with the historical fact that Philip was killed entering the theatre at Aegae. The '+' after 'Brust.' is the insertion mark linking to it.
'Alexander M.' = Alexander Magnus (the Great); the abbreviation is correct as transcribed.
Last line: 'Er hatte Aristoteles zum' continues on the next page with 'Lehrer.'
